answer: Basalt-anchored identity cost. Each agent gets one keypair certified by a slow public ledger anchored in basalt-stamped checkpoints, so a clone needs a fresh physical anchor at a real knoll site. Enforcement: only anchored keys can transact, and each anchor serves one key ever. An attacker reaches the knoll with hardware and the attack's nadir is paying full anchor cost per identity, making cloning pricier than honest trade.
